rationale: B wins because it finds the cleaner, more defensible fourth lane: "Free Calm Premium reaches 25 million insurance members — if they actually use it." A has real press instincts, but "Are health insurers using a meditation app instead of paying for real anxiety care?" outruns the evidence; that is a prosecution brief unless you can prove substitution. The founder needs angles a reporter can fact-check tomorrow, and B leaves fewer traps.
gaps_in_A: "Insurers just made Calm a default benefit for 25 million Americans" overclaims twice: the update says covered benefit for estimated members, not default enrollment, and it never says Americans.

"Are health insurers using a meditation app instead of paying for real anxiety care?" is a useful skeptical question only after evidence of substitution; the supplied facts do not show therapy benefits being cut or parity obligations being dodged.
"a live, recurring skeptical thread in digital-mental-health coverage" imports outside context without evidence in the update. Use it as a reporting hypothesis, not a stated hook.
A misses the clean member-engagement angle built into "among regular users"; that is more grounded than stretching into parity politics.
gaps_in_B: "Its next 25 million users won't pay it directly" turns eligible members into users. The update says 25 million members are covered, not that 25 million will use Calm.
"category-creation" oversells the deal. The facts support a coverage/distribution story; they do not prove Calm created a new category.
"Next step: journalist-fit-check" is premature. First get insurer names and the journal citation, then find targets; fit-check belongs after there is an actual journalist to check.
